extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, in-house counsel, and litigators evaluating post‑grant options
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for choosing among U.S. post‑grant proceedings (IPR, PGR, EPR) by comparing timing, scope, standards, participation, estoppel, outcomes, and strategic uses. Focused on tactical decisions for attacking or defending patent claims at the USPTO or via parallel litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overseeing forum and appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: Which office oversees the proceeding and where appeals lie (PTAB oversees IPRs and PGRs; CRU oversees EPRs, which may be appealed to the PTAB).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know the administrative path: IPRs/PGRs are handled by the Patent Trials and Appeals Board (PTAB). EPRs are handled initially by the Central Reexamination Unit (CRU) and can later be appealed to the PTAB (see M.P.E.P. §2259). This affects procedure, timing, and tactical interactions with PTAB practices (e.g., stays).

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible filing windows / timing constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: When a petition can be filed: PGR must be filed within nine months after grant; IPR may be filed after that period or after PGR termination but not after one year from being served with an infringement complaint; EPRs can be filed at any time during the patent's enforceable life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timing often dictates which forum is available. PGR is exclusive during the nine‑month post‑grant window (35 U.S.C. §321(c), §311(c)). IPRs cannot be filed more than one year after service of an infringement complaint (35 U.S.C. §315(b)). EPRs offer flexibility (35 U.S.C. §302; M.P.E.P. §2209), and can be filed even after or during IPR/PGR if needed (but estoppel interactions apply). Plan filing to preserve or avoid estoppel and to maximize available grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration and speed of proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Expected time from filing to institution and to final decision: PTAB typically decides institution within ~3 months (avg ~6 months from filing) and completes IPR/PGR within one year of institution (extendable 6 months), average ~18 months from petition to completion; EPR institution decisions typically within ~1.5–3 months and average ~15 months to completion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post‑grant proceedings are usually faster than district court litigation (median time to trial >2 years). Consider duration when timing parallel litigation, settlement, or market timelines. Note IPR/PGR can be extended for good cause (35 U.S.C. §316(a)(11)). EPR settlement does not necessarily terminate proceedings, unlike typical IPR/PGR settlements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of review / available statutory grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Which statutory grounds each proceeding can raise: IPR and EPR are limited to novelty (35 U.S.C. §102) and obviousness (§103) based on patents and printed publications; PGR can additionally include patent eligibility (§101), written description/enablement (§112), and double patenting (§121).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose PGR when non‑§102/103 grounds (e.g., §101, §112) are essential and the petition is within the nine‑month window. For questions solely of prior art novelty/obviousness, IPR or EPR may suffice. Remember scope in IPR/PGR is also limited to grounds asserted in the petition (35 U.S.C. §318(a), §328(a)), whereas EPR allows the Office to consider any prior art raising a substantial new question of patentability (M.P.E.P. §2258).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior‑art universe considered
rubrics_metrics.description: The types and sources of prior art the Office may consider: IPR/PGR rely on patents and printed publications asserted in the petition; EPR permits consideration of any prior art, including art found independently by the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPR's broader prior‑art examination power can be an advantage when unasserted or office‑found art is relevant. IPR/PGR petitioners should draft petitions to capture the strongest patents/printed pubs; PGR may allow additional types of challenges beyond patents/printed publications (via §101/§112 issues).

rubrics_metrics.name: Participation rights and posture of parties
rubrics_metrics.description: Which parties may participate and to what extent: IPR and PGR petitioners can participate throughout (reply, discovery, oral hearing, appeal); EPR petitioners have limited participation after filing and the proceeding can become ex parte if the patent owner files a statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If active adversarial participation is desired (e.g., discovery, oral hearing), IPR/PGR are preferable (37 C.F.R. §§42.101, 42.201; 35 U.S.C. §§311–316). EPR is more limited and can be used by patent owners defensively to strengthen claims against newly discovered prior art. Petitioners may remain anonymous in EPRs by using a registered practitioner (M.P.E.P. §2214, §2255).

rubrics_metrics.name: Real party in interest disclosure and anonymity
rubrics_metrics.description: Requirement to identify 'real parties in interest' in IPR/PGR petitions vs. EPR where petitioners can be any party and may remain anonymous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IPR/PGR petitioners must identify all real parties in interest (35 U.S.C. §§312, 322; Samsung v. Netlist guidance), which affects strategy when third parties fund or direct petitions. By contrast, EPRs permit anonymity and broader petitioner types, which can be strategically useful if confidentiality of the challenger is desired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard for institution
rubrics_metrics.description: Different evidentiary thresholds to institute proceedings: PGR requires showing 'more likely than not' that at least one challenged claim is unpatentable; IPR requires a 'reasonable likelihood' of prevailing on at least one claim; EPR requires raising a 'substantial new question of patentability.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These differing standards affect petition drafting and evidentiary burdens (35 U.S.C. §§324(a), 314(a), 303). PGR's 'more likely than not' is stricter than IPR's 'reasonable likelihood.' All administrative standards are easier to meet than district court 'clear and convincing' standard (Microsoft v. i4i). Choose the forum with the institution standard most aligned to your available evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institution/grant rates and typical outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical differences in institution and result rates: IPR/PGR petition institution ~67% and ~50.6% of claims found unpatentable after institution; EPR request grant rate ~92.2% with outcomes including ~21% claims confirmed, ~66% amended, remaining cancelled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statistical outcomes inform forum choice—EPRs have high grant rates and tend to lead to claim amendment rather than cancellation, while IPR/PGR have significant rates of unpatentability findings after institution. Consider likely remedy (cancellation vs amendment vs confirmation) when selecting the forum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estoppel and impacts on later litigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Estoppel effects: IPR/PGR petitioners (and real parties/privies) are barred from later civil actions or PTO proceedings on grounds that could have been raised during PTAB post‑grant proceedings; no estoppel attaches to EPRs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estoppel (35 U.S.C. §§315(e), 325(e)) is a major strategic consideration. Deciding whether to raise all issues before the PTAB (via PGR if available) versus preserving issues for district court by opting for IPR (or forgoing PTAB) requires careful assessment. EPRs don't create estoppel, so they may be used when preserving later litigation options is important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of settlement on proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: How settlements affect ongoing proceedings: settlement of an IPR or PGR typically results in termination of the proceeding; settlement of an EPR does not necessarily terminate the reexamination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties should account for settlement strategy: settling a petition or dispute may not stop an EPR, whereas IPR/PGR settlements commonly lead to termination (35 U.S.C. §§317, 327; but see M.P.E.P. §2209). This can be relevant for patent owners seeking to neutralize challenges or for petitioners seeking finality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estoppel interaction and overlapping proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: How filing one type of proceeding affects others and parallel filings: IPR/PGR may not be instituted if a petitioner already filed a civil action challenging validity; filing an IPR while an EPR is pending can lead to a stay of the EPR; EPRs can be used when PTAB does not institute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider sequencing: filing district court challenges, IPR, PGR, or EPR can trigger bars or stays (35 U.S.C. §§315(a)(1), 325(a)(1); M.P.E.P. §2286.01). Use EPR as a fallback if PTAB denies institution. Be mindful of civil action timing to avoid statutory bars to institution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offensive vs defensive use cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical strategic uses: IPR/PGR commonly used offensively to challenge asserted patents; EPR can be used offensively but also defensively by patent owners to strengthen claims against newly discovered prior art or as a faster alternative to reissue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent owners may proactively request EPRs for high‑value patents to correct or strengthen claims (faster than reissue). Petitioners use IPR/PGR to cancel or narrow claims when facing assertion; use the proceeding that matches tactical goals (eliminate claims, amend claims, clarify validity) and timeframes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical strategic considerations (monitoring and forum choice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Operational strategy guidance: monitor prosecution/grants of competitors, evaluate infringement risk and patent value, review prosecution history and family patents, identify positions to challenge, and strategically choose forum (PGR vs IPR vs EPR vs district court) considering timing, estoppel, scope, and claim construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decision factors include timing windows, estoppel risk, ability to raise §101/§112 issues (favor PGR), participation and discovery needs, likelihood of amendment vs cancellation, and empirical institution/outcome rates. Proactive measures (e.g., EPR for high‑value patents when new art appears) and preserving options in parallel litigation are emphasized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction and preservation of issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Considerations about claim construction differences and preserving issues for district court (e.g., whether to preserve §112 or other issues by foregoing PGR).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategically decide whether to raise all potential invalidity grounds before the PTAB (risking estoppel) or to preserve certain defenses or arguments for district court by choosing a proceeding with narrower scope (e.g., IPR) or forgoing PTAB altogether. The article highlights preserving §112 and related issues by filing an IPR instead of PGR when appropriate.
